events.revisedNote: The actual reading, published this morning, came in at 50.9, missing the 51.5 consensus and easing from June's 51.7, the softest print in several months even though the index stayed in expansion territory.
events.description: A private sector survey of Chinese manufacturing activity, skewed toward smaller, export and tech oriented firms, published a few days ahead of the equivalent services reading. The gauge was rebranded from Caixin to RatingDog this year but keeps the same S&P Global compiled methodology. Since China is the world's second largest economy, a soft print tends to weigh on the yuan and on the growth sensitive Australian and New Zealand dollars given their trade links to China.

A survey of purchasing managers in South Africa's manufacturing sector, compiled by the Bureau for Economic Research for Absa and usually published on the first business day of the month. A reading above 50 signals expansion; a weak print tends to weigh on the rand given the sector's fragile recent run.

events.revisedNote: The actual July print, published this morning, eased to +0.4% y/y (-0.1% m/m) from June's +0.5% y/y, with core inflation steady at +0.3% y/y as fuel prices and airfares fell.
events.description: Switzerland's headline inflation reading from the Federal Statistical Office. With Swiss inflation running well below other major economies, this feeds directly into the SNB's assessment of whether its current policy stance remains appropriate, and it is one of the few scheduled CHF data points before the Bank's next quarterly decision in September.

events.revisedNote: The final reading, published this morning, was confirmed at 51.9, a touch below the 52.0 flash estimate but still the strongest level since April, with German factory output at a four year high.
events.description: The final, revised reading of S&P Global's Eurozone manufacturing survey, usually only a small adjustment from the flash estimate published earlier in the month. A confirmation style release that rarely moves the euro much on its own.

events.revisedNote: The final reading, published this morning, was revised down sharply to 51.9, a four month low and well below both the 52.8 flash estimate and June's 52.5, as new order growth and hiring both cooled.
events.description: The final, revised reading of S&P Global's UK manufacturing survey. Usually a modest adjustment to the flash figure and a secondary mover for sterling, though this month's downward revision marked a notable loss of momentum from the earlier flash estimate.

The Institute for Supply Management's survey of US manufacturing activity, released on the first business day of the month. A reading above 50 signals expansion. Watched as an early, broad based signal of US industrial health, with markets also focused on the prices paid and new orders sub-indices for clues on inflation and demand.

The British Retail Consortium's monthly gauge of average shop prices, published around ten days ahead of the official ONS inflation figures. A useful early steer on the direction of UK consumer price pressure, though it rarely moves sterling much on its own.

A monthly measure of UK retail sales growth compiled by the British Retail Consortium and KPMG, released a few weeks ahead of the official ONS retail sales figures. Gives an early, if noisy, read on the health of the UK consumer.

Statistics Canada's monthly snapshot of the gap between exports and imports of goods. With a large share of Canadian trade tied to the US, this is watched as a barometer of cross border demand and, indirectly, of how tariff related frictions are feeding through to the loonie.

The Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey, a measure of unfilled positions across the US economy that the Federal Reserve watches closely as a gauge of labour market slack. A drop toward pre pandemic levels would support the case for further Fed easing, while a steady reading supports the view that the labour market is cooling only gradually.

A broader measure of new orders placed with US manufacturers than the durable goods report released a few days earlier. Usually a secondary market mover, since much of the durable goods component is already known by the time this is published.

events.event: New Zealand employment change and unemployment rate (Q2)
events.description: Stats NZ's quarterly snapshot of the labour market, covering the change in the number of people employed and the jobless rate. It lands with the Reserve Bank of New Zealand's next policy statement not due until early September, so a soft print would raise questions about how much room the Bank has to keep policy on hold without hurting employment.

The detailed record of policymakers' discussion from the Bank of Japan's June meeting, published with the usual roughly six week lag. Read for clues on how the Board's thinking evolved ahead of its most recent decision to hold rates on 31 July, and on the depth of any dissent for tightening.

A private sector survey of activity in China's much larger services sector, released a few days after the manufacturing equivalent and compiled with the same S&P Global methodology under its new RatingDog name (formerly Caixin). Rounds out the picture of Chinese demand, with relevance for the Australian and New Zealand dollars given their trade exposure to China.

events.event: Eurozone final services and composite PMI (July)
events.description: The final, revised readings of S&P Global's Eurozone services and composite surveys. Usually only a small adjustment from the flash estimate, and a secondary mover for the euro compared with the manufacturing print.

A measure of the prices charged by Eurozone producers at the factory gate, seen as a leading indicator for future consumer price inflation. Less market moving than the CPI print, but still watched by the ECB as part of its broader inflation picture, particularly after July's flash CPI surprised with firmer core inflation.

The final, revised reading of S&P Global's UK services survey, covering the largest part of the UK economy. June marked the sector's steepest contraction since January 2023, so this month's flash rebound to 51.8 is being watched closely for confirmation.

ADP's estimate of private sector payroll growth, released two days ahead of the official US jobs report. Watched closely as an early, if imperfect, signal of how Friday's Nonfarm Payrolls report might land, at a time when the labour market has been showing signs of cooling.

The Institute for Supply Management's survey of the much larger US services sector, released on the third business day of the month. A reading above 50 signals growth; this is one of the most closely watched US releases of the week alongside Friday's jobs report.

The detailed record of the Federal Reserve's 29 July meeting, at which the Fed held its target range at 3.50 to 3.75% in a 9-3 vote, with three policymakers preferring a quarter point increase. Markets will scrutinise the minutes for how deep that hawkish split ran and for any signal on the conditions needed for the Fed's next move, under new Chair Kevin Warsh.

events.event: Fed Governor Lisa Cook speaks on the economic outlook
events.description: Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook addresses an economic luncheon in Anchorage, Alaska. As a sitting voting member of the FOMC, her remarks on inflation, employment and the policy outlook are watched for signals on where she sits relative to the hawkish dissenters from July's meeting.

events.event: Japan average cash earnings and household spending (June)
events.previous: nominal wages +3.2% y/y, real wages +1.4% y/y, household spending -0.4% y/y real (May)
events.description: The Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare's monthly wage survey alongside the household spending report. The Bank of Japan watches wage growth closely as the key input into whether consumption can sustainably support the inflation outlook, particularly after the Bank held rates on 31 July.

The Australian Bureau of Statistics' measure of the gap between exports and imports of goods. A wider surplus is generally supportive for the Australian dollar, and the release is watched closely given China's status as Australia's largest trading partner.

The Reserve Bank of New Zealand's quarterly survey of businesses' and forecasters' expectations for inflation over the next two years. A rise in expectations reinforces the case for a firmer policy stance, and a high reading is generally supportive for the New Zealand dollar.

A monthly gauge of UK house prices based on Lloyds Banking Group's own mortgage approvals data, formerly published under the Halifax name and rebranded as the Lloyds House Price Index from July 2026 onward with the same underlying methodology. Read alongside the Nationwide index as a proxy for household wealth and confidence, which feeds into the Bank of England's broader view of consumer demand.

S&P Global's survey of activity in the UK construction sector. Housebuilding has been the weakest part of the industry recently, with June's reading barely above May's six year low, so this is watched for signs of whether that drag is easing. Typically a minor mover for sterling.

The main measure of consumer spending across the Eurozone. A high reading strengthens the euro, while a low one weakens it, since consumer demand is a key input into the ECB's growth and inflation outlook.

The number of people filing for unemployment benefits for the first time that week. A high frequency, early read on the US labour market, usually a minor mover unless it deviates sharply from expectations, and watched closely this week just a day ahead of the July jobs report.

China customs data on the gap between exports and imports. June's surplus was the second largest on record, driven by surging chip and AI data centre hardware related exports; the release is watched for whether that export strength has been sustained into July, with knock on relevance for the Australian and New Zealand dollars.

events.event: Canada Labour Force Survey: employment and unemployment rate (July)
events.description: Statistics Canada's monthly labour market report, covering the change in employment and the jobless rate. Released alongside the US jobs report, it is watched for signs of how much slack is building in the Canadian economy while the Bank of Canada remains on hold until its next meeting in September.

events.event: US Nonfarm Payrolls, average hourly earnings and unemployment rate (July)
events.consensus: around 130,000 jobs, unemployment rate unchanged at 4.2%
events.description: The US Department of Labor's monthly employment report, the single most closely watched release on the calendar. June's payrolls figure of just 57,000 was well below expectations and reopened debate about the timing of the Fed's next move; a second soft print in July would add to that debate, while a strong number would support the more hawkish tone struck by some FOMC members at July's meeting.
